modules.title: Foundations: How UX Design Works
modules.overview: Learn what UX design really is, the five components of usability, and the design thinking process professionals use. Set up a low-cost toolkit, choose a practice project, and learn to run research ethically.

lessons.title: What UX design is and the problems it solves
objectives: Define user experience (UX) and explain how it differs from user interface (UI) design
Name the five quality components of usability: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction
Spot a UX problem in an app you use every day and describe who it hurts
Explain why good UX builds trust, especially in money and learning apps

blocks.text: **User experience (UX)** is everything a person feels and does while using a product: finding it, learning it, getting a task done, recovering from a mistake, and deciding whether to come back. A **UX designer** studies real users, finds where they struggle, and shapes the product so the task becomes easy, quick and safe. The product can be a mobile app, a website, a USSD menu, or even a paper form at a bank.

**User interface (UI)** is the part you can see and touch: buttons, colours, fonts, icons, screens. UI is one part of UX. A beautiful screen can still give a bad experience if the button you need is hidden, the words are confusing, or the app forgets what you typed when the network drops. In this course you will spend most of your time on the thinking that comes before colours: understanding people, organising content, sketching layouts and testing them.

blocks.name: mobile-ux
blocks.alt: A person using a large phone screen with interface elements around it
blocks.caption: UX covers the whole experience on the phone, not only how the screen looks.

blocks.text: Usability: the measurable core of UX
Jakob Nielsen of the Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) describes **usability** with five quality components. You will use these words for the rest of the course, so learn them well:

head: Component
Plain question
Local example
rows: Can a first-time user do the basic task easily?
Can a new user send money on a wallet app on day one without help?
Once she knows it, how fast can she do the task?
Does buying airtime take 4 taps or 12?
After weeks away, can she still use it?
Can she find the bill payment menu again after a month?
How many mistakes, how serious, how easy to fix?
Does the app warn her before sending to the wrong account number?
Does she feel calm or anxious when the transfer is processing?

blocks.text: Usability is about whether people **can** use a product. **Utility** is whether the product does something they **need**. NN/g puts it simply: useful means usable plus has utility. An app that looks easy but does not let a market woman record credit sales has no utility for her.
Problems UX design solves

items: **Drop-off:** people start signing up, then give up at a long or confusing form.
**Costly mistakes:** a transfer goes to the wrong account because the app did not show the account name before confirming.
**Support overload:** staff answer the same WhatsApp questions every day because the app does not explain itself.
**Lost trust:** a payment screen spins with no message, so the user does not know if her money left her account and pays twice.
**Exclusion:** small text, low contrast or English-only wording shuts out older users, people with poor eyesight or users with less schooling.

blocks.title: Worked example: the transfer that went quiet
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Onitsha sends 25,000 naira (approximate) to her supplier using a mobile banking app. After she enters her PIN, the screen shows a spinning circle for about 40 seconds on a weak network, then returns to the home screen with no message.
steps: Amaka does not know whether the money left. She checks her balance, but the debit has not shown yet.
She tries again. Both transfers eventually go through, so she has sent 50,000 naira instead of 25,000.
A UX designer studying this would name the problem: poor **visibility of system status** and no protection against a **duplicate transaction**.
Possible design fixes: show a clear 'Processing, do not retry' message, a transaction reference, and a warning if the same amount is sent to the same account within a few minutes.
blocks.result: The fix is not a new colour. It is clear feedback at the right moment and a guard against a likely error. That is UX work: it reduces losses, support calls and fear.

blocks.text: Why UX matters for trust

People judge an app quickly. When a fintech, school or health app feels confusing, many users assume it is unsafe. Clear wording, honest status messages, predictable buttons and easy ways to undo mistakes all signal that the organisation respects its users. For the WODDI community, good UX can mean the difference between a mother finishing an online course and giving up because she could not find her certificate.

blocks.title: UX versus UI
items: UX (experience)
UI (interface)
blocks.caption: UX decides what the product must do and in what order; UI decides how each screen looks.

blocks.text: UX work also has a business side. When fewer people abandon a sign-up form, more customers complete it. When the app explains itself, support staff spend less time answering the same questions. These are results you can measure, and later in this course you will learn to report them clearly.

blocks.title: UX is not only for big companies
blocks.text: A small business WhatsApp catalogue, a church registration form or a school fees page all have a user experience. The same methods you learn here work for all of them.

takeaways: UX is the whole experience of using a product; UI is the visible screens and controls
Usability has five components: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction
A product must be both usable and useful (have utility)
Many UX fixes are about clear feedback and preventing costly errors, not decoration

activity.title: Find a real UX problem
steps: Pick one app you use weekly (for example a bank, wallet, ride-hailing or shopping app).
Do one common task in it, such as buying airtime or tracking an order, and note every moment you hesitate.
Write down one problem and which usability component it hurts (learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors or satisfaction).
Write one sentence describing who is most affected (for example older users, first-time users, people on weak networks).
Take a screenshot of the screen where the problem happens, hiding any balances or personal details.
activity.evidence: One screenshot (personal details hidden) with a short note naming the problem, the usability component and the affected user.

lessons.title: The UX process and the words designers use
objectives: Describe the five design thinking stages: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test
Relate design thinking to the Double Diamond (discover, define, develop, deliver)
Use core UX vocabulary correctly: persona, journey map, pain point, information architecture, wireframe, prototype, usability test
Explain why the process repeats instead of running once

blocks.text: UX designers follow a process so that decisions come from evidence about users, not from personal taste. The most widely taught version is **design thinking**, popularised by the Stanford d.school and IDEO. It has five stages. They are not strict steps: teams move back and forth as they learn.

blocks.title: Design thinking stages
items: Empathise with users
Define the problem
Ideate solutions
Prototype quickly
Test with users
blocks.caption: Testing sends you back to earlier stages, so the cycle repeats until the design works for real users.

head: Stage
What you do
Typical output
rows: Observe and interview real users in their setting
Turn what you learned into a clear problem statement
Persona, problem statement, 'How might we' question
Generate many possible solutions before choosing
Build a cheap, quick version to try
Paper sketch, Figma wireframe, clickable prototype
Watch real users try the prototype

blocks.text: The Double Diamond

The UK Design Council describes a similar process called the **Double Diamond**. The first diamond is about the problem: **Discover** (go wide, research) then **Define** (narrow to the real problem). The second diamond is about the solution: **Develop** (go wide, many ideas) then **Deliver** (narrow to one, test and launch). The shape reminds you to open up before you close down, twice. Many teams fail by jumping straight to a solution before they understand the problem.

blocks.name: design-thinking
blocks.alt: A person standing beside a large lightbulb and connected idea shapes
blocks.caption: Design thinking moves from understanding people to ideas you can test.

blocks.text: Core vocabulary

items: **User research:** methods for learning about users, such as interviews, observation, surveys and testing.
**Pain point:** a specific moment of frustration, delay, cost or fear in a user's task. Example: 'I cannot find my receipt after paying school fees.'
**Persona:** a short, realistic profile of a type of user, built from research, not imagination. It includes goals, frustrations, devices and context.
**Journey map:** a timeline of the steps a user takes to reach a goal, with what she does, thinks and feels at each step.
**Information architecture (IA):** how content is organised, grouped and labelled so people can find things.
**User flow:** the path of screens and decisions a user goes through to finish one task.
**Wireframe:** a simple black-and-white layout of a screen showing structure, not colours.
**Prototype:** a version of the design people can click or tap through to test the flow.
**Usability test:** watching real users try to complete tasks with your design while you note where they struggle.
**Heuristic evaluation:** an expert review of a design against recognised rules of thumb, such as Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics.
**Accessibility:** designing so people with disabilities, including poor eyesight, hearing loss or limited hand movement, can use the product.

blocks.title: Worked example: from pain point to 'How might we'
blocks.context: For example, Funke volunteers for a women's learning network. Members keep sending WhatsApp messages asking where to download their course certificates.
steps: Empathise: Funke speaks with 6 members by phone. Four of them say they looked under 'Profile' first; two gave up after 5 minutes.
Define: she writes a problem statement: 'Members who finish a course cannot find their certificate because it sits under Settings, which they do not associate with achievements.'
She turns it into a question: 'How might we help members find their certificate in under 30 seconds right after finishing?'
Ideate: she lists 8 ideas, including a 'Download certificate' button on the course completion screen and a 'My certificates' item in the main menu.
Prototype and test: she sketches two options on paper and shows them to 5 members, timing how long each takes to find the certificate.
blocks.result: The 'How might we' question keeps the team focused on the user's goal and gives a clear target (under 30 seconds) to test against.

blocks.title: Write problem statements about users, not features
blocks.text: A weak statement says 'We need a new menu.' A strong one says who struggles, with what task, and why: 'First-time users cannot find X because Y.' The solution comes later.
Where this course fits

This course follows the same path. Module 1 covers the foundations. Module 2 takes you through empathise and define (interviews, personas, journey maps) and then into ideate and prototype (information architecture, user flows and Figma wireframes). Module 3 covers testing and quality: Nielsen's heuristics, accessibility, and usability testing with real users. Module 4 turns your work into a case study you can show to an employer, client or community leader.

Notice that the process is a loop. A usability test almost always reveals something you did not expect, which sends you back to define the problem more sharply or to try new ideas. This is normal and healthy. Professional teams plan for several rounds of testing and improvement, called **iteration**.

takeaways: Design thinking: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test, repeated as needed
The Double Diamond reminds you to explore widely before narrowing, for both problem and solution
A persona and a journey map are built from research, not guesses
Good problem statements name the user, the task and the reason it fails

activity.title: Write your first problem statement
steps: Use the problem you found in the previous lesson's activity.
Write it as: '[Type of user] cannot [task] because [reason].'
Turn it into one 'How might we...?' question with a measurable target (time, number of taps, or error count).
List at least 5 different ideas that could answer the question, without judging them yet.
Circle the two ideas you would prototype first and write one line on why.
activity.evidence: A note or photo of your problem statement, 'How might we' question and idea list with two circled.

lessons.title: Your toolkit, practice project and research ethics
objectives: Set up a low-cost UX toolkit: paper, a phone, Figma and free form tools
Choose a realistic practice project you will carry through the whole course
Prepare an informed consent script for interviews and tests
Handle research data in line with basic privacy principles, including Nigeria's data protection law

blocks.text: You do not need an expensive laptop to start UX work. Much of the early work is done with paper, a pen and conversations. You will need a computer for the Figma lessons in Module 2, but you can borrow one or use a cyber café for those sessions. Plan your data use: Figma runs in a browser and needs a steady connection, while interviews and paper sketches need no data at all.
A practical starter toolkit

head: Tool
What it is for
Cost
rows: A4 paper, pencil, marker, sticky notes
Sketching screens, journey maps, grouping research notes
Voice recording (with consent), photos of sketches, testing apps

blocks.name: design-tools
blocks.alt: A designer surrounded by simple design tools
blocks.caption: Paper, a phone and one browser tool are enough to practise the full UX process.

blocks.text: Choose one practice project
You will learn faster if every lesson builds on the same project. Choose something small, real and close to you, where you can easily reach 5 to 8 users. Good choices include:

items: Redesigning the sign-up or booking flow for a local salon, clinic or tailoring business that takes orders on WhatsApp.
Improving how members of a church, cooperative or association register for events.
Designing a simple app screen flow for a market seller to record credit sales.
Improving how learners find lessons and certificates on a learning platform you use.

blocks.title: Keep it small
blocks.text: Do not choose 'build a new bank app'. Choose one task, such as 'book an appointment' or 'download a certificate'. A small project done well teaches more than a large one left half finished.
Research ethics: consent first

When you interview or test with people, you are collecting personal information. Treat it with care. Always get **informed consent**: the person understands what you are doing, why, how long it takes, what you will record, and that they can stop at any time without any penalty. Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), sets rules for processing personal data, including having a lawful basis such as consent and keeping data secure. You are not a lawyer, but you should follow the basic principles: collect only what you need, keep it safe, and delete it when you are done.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 60-second consent script
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is about to interview a tailor in Kaduna about how customers book fittings.
steps: She says: 'Thank you for helping. I am learning UX design and studying how customers book fittings. It will take about 20 minutes.'
'There are no right or wrong answers. I am testing ideas, not testing you.'
'May I record our voices so I do not miss anything? Only I will listen, and I will delete it after writing notes. I will not use your name in my report.'
'You can skip any question or stop at any time.'
She waits for a clear 'yes', notes the date and that consent was given, and only then starts the recording.
blocks.result: The participant feels respected and relaxed, and Zainab has a clear record that consent was given before recording began.

blocks.title: Before any research session
items: Purpose explained clearly
Time needed stated
Recording permission asked
Right to stop explained
Names removed from notes
blocks.caption: Run through this checklist every time before you interview or test someone.

blocks.title: Protect people and yourself
blocks.text: Never ask for bank PINs, passwords, BVN or account numbers during research, even in a test prototype. Use fake data such as 'Account: 0123456789'. Meet participants in public or familiar places, or by phone, and tell someone where you are going.
Recruiting the right people

Your participants should match the people who will really use the product. If your project is a booking flow for a salon, talk to the salon's customers, not your designer friends. Aim for a mix: some confident smartphone users and some who find apps harder, different ages, and, if relevant, people who prefer Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo or Yoruba. A short screening question such as 'How did you last book an appointment?' helps you choose people with real experience of the task. Thank participants for their time; a small token such as airtime is common, but say clearly that it does not depend on what they say.

Store recordings and notes in a folder protected by a password or phone lock. Use codes like 'P1, P2' instead of names in your findings. If you photograph someone's screen, ask first and crop out balances, phone numbers and messages.

takeaways: Paper, a smartphone and Figma's free plan are enough to start
Choose one small, real practice project with users you can reach
Always get informed consent before recording or testing
Collect only what you need, use participant codes, and never collect PINs or BVNs

activity.title: Prepare your project and consent kit
steps: Write your project in one sentence: 'I will improve how [users] [do task] on [product].'
List 5 to 8 people you could realistically interview who match those users.
Write your own consent script in your own words, in English or the language your users prefer.
Create a free Figma account and open a blank design file to confirm it works on your device.
Create a protected folder on your phone or computer for research notes.
activity.evidence: Your one-sentence project statement, list of possible participants (first names or codes only), and written consent script.

quiz.q: A wallet app looks beautiful, but users often send money to the wrong account because it does not show the account name before confirming. Which usability component is most affected?
quiz.explain: The problem is a serious, preventable mistake. The 'errors' component asks how many mistakes users make, how serious they are and how easily they recover.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the difference between UX and UI?
options: UX is for websites and UI is for apps
UI is the whole experience; UX is the colours and fonts
UX covers the whole experience of using a product; UI is the visible screens and controls
They mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explain: UI is one part of UX. UX includes research, flow, content and how people feel, not only the visible interface.

quiz.q: Chioma has interviewed 6 users and now writes: 'New members cannot find their receipts because they are under Settings.' Which design thinking stage is she in?
quiz.explain: Turning research findings into a clear problem statement is the Define stage.

quiz.q: In the Double Diamond, what happens in the first diamond?
options: Building and launching the final product
Exploring widely to discover, then narrowing to define the real problem
quiz.explain: The first diamond is about the problem: Discover (go wide) then Define (narrow down).

quiz.q: During a test of a payment prototype, which data should Kemi use?
options: The participant's real bank account number
Fake sample data such as a made-up account number
The participant's BVN to make it realistic
quiz.explain: Never collect PINs, BVNs or real account numbers in research. Fake data tests the design just as well and protects people.

quiz.q: Which practice project is the best size for this course?
options: Build a complete new banking app
Redesign every page of a large website
Improve how customers book a fitting with a local tailor
Design an app for all of Nigeria's markets
quiz.explain: A small project focused on one task, with users you can reach, lets you complete the full process well.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Research to Prototype
modules.overview: Move through the core UX workflow on your own practice project. You will interview users and build a persona, map the journey and structure the content, then turn it all into wireframes and a clickable Figma prototype.

lessons.title: User interviews and research-based personas
objectives: Write an interview guide with open, non-leading questions about past behaviour
Run a 20 to 30 minute user interview and take useful notes
Group interview notes into themes using affinity mapping
Build a persona from real findings, not imagination

blocks.text: Interviews are the most useful research method for a beginner. In 20 to 30 minutes of one-to-one conversation you learn how people really do a task today, what gets in their way, and what words they use. For a small project, **5 to 8 interviews** with people who match your target users usually reveal the main patterns. When you start hearing the same stories again and again, you have enough to move forward.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people sitting across from each other having a conversation
blocks.caption: A good interview feels like a relaxed conversation guided by your prepared questions.

blocks.text: Ask about the past, not the future

People are poor at predicting what they will do, but good at describing what they did. 'Would you use an app to book fittings?' gets a polite yes. 'Tell me about the last time you booked a fitting' gets the truth: she called three times, the tailor did not pick up, she went in person and waited an hour. Ask **open questions** that start with what, how, tell me about, walk me through. Avoid **leading questions** that suggest an answer.

head: Avoid (leading or closed)
Ask instead (open)
rows: Don't you find the app confusing?
Walk me through the last time you used the app.
Would you like a reminder feature?
How do you remember your appointments now?
How did you decide whether to pay?
Do you use WhatsApp to order?
Tell me how you placed your last order, step by step.

blocks.text: Structure of an interview guide

items: **Warm-up (2 to 3 minutes):** consent script, simple questions about her day or work.
**Context (5 minutes):** how she currently handles the task, which tools, how often.
**Deep dive (10 to 15 minutes):** the last time she did the task, step by step. Ask 'What happened next?' and 'How did that feel?'
**Pain points (5 minutes):** 'What is the most annoying part?' 'What have you tried to make it easier?'
**Wrap-up (2 minutes):** 'Is there anything I should have asked?' Thank her.

blocks.title: Listen more than you talk
blocks.text: Silence is useful. After she answers, wait a few seconds before your next question. People often add the most honest detail when they fill the pause. Follow up with 'Why was that?' or 'Can you show me?'
From notes to themes: affinity mapping

After the interviews, write each separate observation or quote on its own sticky note or small piece of paper: one idea per note. Spread them out and group notes that are about the same thing. Name each group with a short theme, such as 'Unsure if payment worked' or 'Prefers voice notes to typing'. This is called **affinity mapping** or affinity diagramming. Count how many participants mention each theme. A theme mentioned by 5 out of 6 people matters more than one mentioned once.

blocks.title: Worked example: interviews for a salon booking flow
blocks.context: For example, Blessing is redesigning how customers book appointments at a hair salon in Ikeja that currently takes bookings only by WhatsApp chat. She interviews 6 customers (P1 to P6).
steps: She writes 47 notes from the 6 interviews and groups them into 5 themes.
Theme 1, 'Waiting for a reply': 5 of 6 said they wait hours for the salon to confirm a slot on WhatsApp.
Theme 2, 'Price surprise': 4 of 6 said they learned the full price for braids only at the salon.
Theme 3, 'Wants to see the stylist's work first': 3 of 6 asked friends for photos.
Themes 4 and 5 were mentioned by only 1 or 2 people, so she notes them but does not prioritise them.
She concludes that instant slot confirmation and clear prices are the two biggest needs.
blocks.result: Instead of guessing, Blessing now has evidence: the booking design must show available times and prices up front. Five of six users told her so.

blocks.text: Building a persona

A **persona** summarises a group of similar users as one realistic person, so the team can ask 'Would this work for her?' A good persona is based on your themes. Include: a name and photo placeholder, age range, location and device, goals related to your task, frustrations (pain points), current tools and habits, and one or two real quotes from interviews. Keep it to one page. Avoid stereotypes and irrelevant details such as favourite colour unless your research showed they matter.

blocks.title: From interviews to persona
items: Interview 5 to 8 users
Write one note per idea
Group notes into themes
Count who said what
Write a one-page persona
blocks.caption: Each persona detail should trace back to something real users said or did.

blocks.title: Proto-personas are guesses
blocks.text: A persona written before any research is called a proto-persona or assumption persona. It can help you plan research, but label it clearly and replace it with real findings as soon as you have them.

If you have time for only a few interviews, still do them. Even three honest conversations will correct assumptions that would otherwise shape your whole design. Write up your notes the same day while you still remember tone, gestures and the exact words people used.

takeaways: Interview 5 to 8 people who match your users; stop when patterns repeat
Ask open questions about real past behaviour, not hypothetical futures
Affinity mapping turns scattered notes into counted themes
Personas must be built from research and fit on one page

activity.title: Interview and synthesise
steps: Write an interview guide of 8 to 10 open questions for your practice project.
Interview at least 3 people (5 is better), using your consent script from Module 1.
Write one observation or quote per note, then group them into 3 to 6 themes.
Record how many participants mentioned each theme.
Write a one-page persona using only what you heard.
activity.evidence: Your interview guide, a photo of your grouped notes with theme names and counts, and your one-page persona.

lessons.title: Journey maps, information architecture and user flows
objectives: Draw a current-state journey map showing actions, thoughts, feelings and pain points
Organise content and menus using simple information architecture and card sorting
Draw a user flow for one task, including decision points and error paths
Choose which pain points to design for first

blocks.text: Your persona tells you **who** you are designing for. The next three tools show **how** she moves through the task today and how the new design should be organised. A **journey map** shows the whole experience over time. **Information architecture** decides where things live and what they are called. A **user flow** shows the exact screens and choices for one task.
Journey maps

A journey map is a timeline from left to right. Across the top you list the **stages** of the experience. Under each stage you add rows: what she **does**, what she **thinks**, how she **feels** (often drawn as a line going up and down), and the **pain points** and **opportunities**. NN/g distinguishes current-state maps, which show how things are today, from future-state maps, which show how you want them to be. Start with current-state, built from your interviews.

head: Stage
Does
Thinks or feels
Pain point
rows: Scrolls salon's WhatsApp status for styles
Relieved but unsure it is confirmed

blocks.name: user-flow
blocks.alt: Connected boxes and arrows showing a path through screens
blocks.caption: Journey maps and user flows make the path through a task visible, so gaps stand out.

blocks.text: Look along the 'feels' row for the low points. Those are where design can help most. In the salon example, the lowest points are waiting for a price, not knowing if the booking is confirmed, and double-booking. All three point to one opportunity: a booking page showing prices, live available slots and an automatic confirmation.
Information architecture and card sorting

**Information architecture (IA)** is the structure behind menus and navigation. Good IA uses the words your users use and groups things the way they expect. A simple way to learn their mental model is **card sorting**: write each content item on a card (for example 'Braids prices', 'Book appointment', 'Stylist photos', 'Opening hours', 'Cancel booking'), then ask 5 or more users to group the cards and name each group. In an **open** card sort users create their own group names; in a **closed** sort you give them the categories. Where most people put a card tells you where to place it in your menu.

blocks.title: Use their words, not yours
blocks.text: If users call it 'hairstyles' and the business calls it 'services', the menu should say 'Hairstyles'. Labels that match the real world are one of Nielsen's heuristics, which you will study in Module 3.
User flows

A **user flow** shows each screen (drawn as a rectangle), each decision (a diamond), and the arrows between them, for one task from start to finish. It forces you to think about what happens when things go wrong: the chosen slot is already taken, the payment fails, the network drops. Draw the 'happy path' first, then add the error paths.

blocks.title: Worked example: flow for 'Book a braiding appointment'
blocks.context: For example, Blessing turns her salon research into a user flow before drawing any screens.
steps: Entry: customer taps a booking link shared on the salon's WhatsApp status.
Screen 1, Choose style: list of hairstyles with photos and starting prices.
Screen 2, Choose date and time: only free slots shown.
Decision: is the slot still free when she taps Confirm? If no, show 'Sorry, that time was just taken' and return to Screen 2 with her style kept.
Screen 3, Details: name and phone number only, two fields.
Screen 4, Pay deposit: through a payment provider such as Paystack, with a clear amount.
Decision: payment successful? If no, show the reason and a 'Try again' button without losing her booking. If yes, go to Screen 5.
Screen 5, Confirmation: date, time, stylist, amount paid, reference number, and 'Add to calendar'.
blocks.result: The flow has 5 screens and 2 decision points, and every pain point from the journey map now has a matching design answer: prices shown, live slots, confirmation with reference.

blocks.title: Booking happy path
items: Choose style and price
Pick free slot
Enter name and phone
Pay deposit
See confirmation
blocks.caption: The happy path should be short; error paths branch off it and return the user without losing her progress.

blocks.text: Before you move on, check your flow against the journey map. Every pain point you chose to fix should have a clear answer somewhere in the flow. If a pain point has no answer, either add a step or decide openly that you will not solve it in this version. Also check the entry point: how does she arrive? A link in a WhatsApp status, a QR code on the salon mirror and a Google Maps listing are all different starting points, and each may need a slightly different first screen.
Keep the number of steps as small as possible, and ask only for information you truly need. Every extra field is a chance for her to give up, especially on a small phone with a slow connection.

takeaways: Journey maps show stages, actions, feelings and pain points over time
Card sorting reveals how users group and name content
User flows show screens, decisions and error paths for one task
Design first for the lowest emotional points on the journey map

activity.title: Map the journey and the flow
steps: Draw a current-state journey map for your persona with 4 to 6 stages, using your interview notes.
Mark the two lowest points on the feelings line and write one opportunity for each.
Run a quick card sort with 3 or more people using 10 to 15 content cards.
Draw a user flow for your main task, including at least one error path.
Photograph all three.
activity.evidence: Photos of your journey map, card sort results (groups and names) and user flow with at least one error path.

lessons.title: Wireframes and clickable prototypes in Figma
objectives: Explain low, mid and high fidelity and when to use each
Sketch paper wireframes, then build mid-fidelity wireframes in Figma using frames, shapes and text
Apply basic mobile layout rules: visual hierarchy, thumb reach and touch target size
Link screens into a clickable prototype and share it for testing

blocks.text: A **wireframe** is a simple layout of a screen. It shows what goes where: headings, images, buttons, fields. It deliberately leaves out colour and polish, so people react to structure and flow rather than taste. A **prototype** links screens together so someone can tap through the task as if it were real.

head: Fidelity
What it looks like
Best for
rows: Pencil sketches on paper, boxes and squiggles
Grey boxes and real text in a tool like Figma
Testing flow and content with users
Real colours, fonts, images and icons
Final checks and handing over to developers

blocks.text: Start on paper

Fold an A4 sheet into 4 or 8 parts and sketch a different version of the same screen in each part. This technique, often called **Crazy 8s**, gives you eight quick ideas in about eight minutes. Pick the best parts of each and sketch one clean version of every screen in your user flow.

blocks.name: wireframing
blocks.alt: A designer arranging grey boxes that represent a screen layout
blocks.caption: Wireframes show structure with simple boxes so feedback stays on layout and flow.

blocks.text: Building wireframes in Figma

items: Create a new design file. Press **F** (or **A**) for the Frame tool and choose a phone preset from the right panel, such as an Android or iPhone size.
Use **R** for rectangles (image placeholders, buttons, input fields) and **T** for text. Write real labels, such as 'Book appointment', not 'Button'.
Keep everything in shades of grey. Make the most important action the darkest, largest element on the screen.
Select a group of items and press **Shift + A** to add Auto layout, which keeps spacing even when text changes.
Duplicate the frame for each screen in your user flow and name each frame clearly, for example '02 Choose time'.

blocks.text: Mobile layout rules that matter

items: **Visual hierarchy:** one main action per screen, placed where the eye lands. Size, weight and position show what matters most.
**Thumb reach:** most people hold the phone in one hand. Put the main button in the lower half of the screen where the thumb reaches easily.
**Touch targets:** Apple's guidelines recommend at least 44 by 44 points and Google's Material Design at least 48 by 48 dp for tappable items. Small links next to each other cause mis-taps.
**Consistent spacing:** many designers use multiples of 8 pixels (8, 16, 24, 32) so screens feel orderly.
**Readable text:** body text large enough to read without zooming, with short lines and plain words.

blocks.text: Making it clickable

In Figma, switch to the **Prototype** tab in the right panel. Select a button, drag the small circle that appears onto the screen it should open, and choose 'On tap' and 'Navigate to'. Repeat for each step in the flow, including a 'Back' link. Press the **Present** (play) button to try it. Use **Share** to copy a link, which participants can open in a browser or the Figma mobile app.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing two layouts for the time picker
blocks.context: For example, Blessing builds two mid-fidelity versions of the 'Choose time' screen for the salon and asks 5 customers to book Saturday at 10am.
steps: Version A shows a calendar month view; the customer taps a date, then sees time slots below.
Version B shows the next 7 days as a row of buttons with time slots underneath, all on one screen.
With Version A, 3 of 5 customers scrolled past the slots and needed help. Average time: about 50 seconds.
With Version B, 5 of 5 booked without help. Average time: about 20 seconds.
She keeps Version B and moves the 'Confirm' button into the lower third of the screen for easier thumb reach.
blocks.result: Mid-fidelity wireframes let Blessing compare two ideas in one afternoon, before any money was spent on development.

blocks.title: Fidelity grows step by step
items: Paper sketches
Grey Figma wireframes
Clickable prototype
Test and improve
Visual design
blocks.caption: Add detail only after the structure has been tested, because changes are cheapest early.

blocks.text: Common beginner mistakes at this stage: jumping to colours and logos before the flow works, using placeholder text like 'Lorem' that hides content problems, forgetting empty and error states (what does the screen show when there are no free slots?), and designing only for a large new phone. Check every screen at a small Android size too, since many of your users will have one.

blocks.title: Name frames and layers
blocks.text: Give every frame a number and a name, and keep one page in your Figma file called 'Flow' with all screens in order. When you share the file, testers and reviewers can follow it without your help, and you can find things quickly when you iterate.

blocks.title: Design for low data
blocks.text: Many users have limited data. Note in your wireframe where images can be small or optional, and keep critical text and buttons visible even before images load.

takeaways: Start with paper sketches, then build grey mid-fidelity wireframes in Figma
Use real labels and make the main action obvious and easy to reach
Tappable items should be large: about 44 to 48 units by platform guidelines
Link screens in Figma's Prototype tab and share the link for testing

activity.title: Build your clickable prototype
steps: Do one round of Crazy 8s for the most important screen in your flow.
Sketch every screen of your user flow on paper.
Build mid-fidelity wireframes of those screens in Figma with real labels.
Link the screens in the Prototype tab, including at least one error or back path.
Tap through it yourself on your phone and fix any broken links.
activity.evidence: Photo of your Crazy 8s sheet, screenshots of your Figma frames, and the share link to your clickable prototype.

quiz.q: Which interview question is best for learning how a customer really books a tailor?
options: Would you use an app to book a tailor?
Don't you hate waiting for tailors?
Tell me about the last time you booked a fitting, step by step.
quiz.explain: Open questions about real past behaviour give honest detail. The others are hypothetical or leading.

quiz.q: After 6 interviews, Ada has 52 notes. What should she do next?
options: Design the home screen straight away
Group notes into themes and count how many people mentioned each
Delete notes that only one person mentioned
Write a persona from her own experience
quiz.explain: Affinity mapping groups notes into themes; counting mentions shows which problems matter most.

quiz.q: On a journey map, where should a designer usually focus first?
options: The stages where the user feels best
The lowest points on the feelings line, where pain points cluster
Whichever stage has the most text
quiz.explain: The emotional low points show where the experience fails users most and where design can help most.

quiz.q: Users in a card sort keep putting 'Braids prices' under a group they call 'Hairstyles'. The business menu says 'Services'. What should the designer do?
options: Keep 'Services' because the business chose it
Use both labels for the same item
quiz.explain: Labels should match users' mental models and language, not internal business terms.

quiz.q: Why are mid-fidelity wireframes usually grey with no colours?
options: So people react to structure and flow, not visual taste
quiz.explain: Leaving out colour keeps feedback on layout, content and flow, which are cheaper to fix early.

quiz.q: In a phone wireframe, where should the main 'Confirm booking' button usually go?
options: Tiny, at the very top corner
In the lower part of the screen, large enough to tap easily
quiz.explain: Most people use one thumb; the lower area is easier to reach, and large touch targets reduce mis-taps.

modules.title: Quality, Ethics and Measurement
modules.overview: Check your design against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics, make it accessible and honest using WCAG basics and ethical principles, and prove it works by testing with real users and measuring results.

lessons.title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics and expert review
objectives: Name and explain Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics with a local example of each
Run a heuristic review of your own prototype or a real app
Rate each problem using Nielsen's 0 to 4 severity scale
Avoid the most common beginner design mistakes

blocks.text: Before you test with users, you can catch many problems yourself by reviewing the design against proven rules of thumb. The best known are **Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics**, first published in 1994 and still used by design teams worldwide. A review against them is called a **heuristic evaluation**. It is quick and cheap, but it does not replace testing with real users; it finds different problems.

head: Heuristic
What it means
Example you may know
rows: Always tell users what is happening, quickly
A transfer screen showing 'Processing' then 'Successful' with a reference
2. Match between system and the real world
Use users' words and familiar ideas
A 'Cancel' button before final payment confirmation
Same words and patterns everywhere; follow platform norms
The back arrow always in the same place on every screen
Showing the recipient's account name before you confirm a transfer
Show options instead of making users remember
A list of recent beneficiaries instead of retyping account numbers
Remove anything that does not help the task
A payment screen without banners competing with the 'Pay' button
9. Help users recognise, diagnose, and recover from errors
Plain error messages that say what to do
'Network is slow. Your money has not left your account. Try again.'
A short in-app guide or help link on the screen where people get stuck

blocks.name: ui-analysis
blocks.alt: A person examining a large interface with a magnifying glass
blocks.caption: A heuristic review checks every screen against proven usability principles.

blocks.text: How to run a heuristic review

items: Choose the task to review, for example 'book an appointment' in your prototype.
Go through the task screen by screen at least twice: once to understand the flow, once to look for problems.
For each problem, write: the screen, what is wrong, which heuristic it breaks, and a suggested fix.
Give each problem a severity rating from 0 to 4 (see below).
If possible, ask 2 or 3 other people to review separately, then combine lists. Different reviewers find different problems.

blocks.text: Severity ratings
Nielsen suggests rating each problem so the team fixes the worst first. Severity depends on how often it happens, how much it hurts the user when it does, and whether users can get around it.

items: **0:** not a usability problem.
**1:** cosmetic only; fix if there is time.
**2:** minor; low priority.
**3:** major; important to fix, high priority.
**4:** usability catastrophe; must fix before release.

blocks.title: Worked example: reviewing a school fees payment page
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi reviews a private school's online fees page used by parents in Port Harcourt.
steps: Problem 1: after tapping 'Pay', the page shows a blank white screen for up to 30 seconds. Breaks heuristic 1 (visibility of system status). Parents might pay twice. Severity 4.
Problem 2: the student ID field accepts any text and only shows 'Invalid input' after payment fails. Breaks heuristics 5 and 9. Severity 3.
Problem 3: the menu says 'Remittance' for payments and 'Ledger' for receipts. Breaks heuristic 2. Severity 2.
Problem 4: two different button colours are used for the same 'Next' action. Breaks heuristic 4. Severity 1.
She sorts by severity and recommends fixing problems 1 and 2 before the next term's payments open.
blocks.result: Four problems found in under an hour, ranked so the school knows exactly what to fix first and why.

blocks.title: Fix order by severity
items: 4 Catastrophe: fix now
3 Major: fix soon
2 Minor: plan it
1 Cosmetic: if time
blocks.caption: Spend your limited time on the problems that cause the most harm to users first.

blocks.text: Common beginner mistakes

items: Designing for yourself instead of your persona.
Too many choices on one screen, so nothing stands out.
Icons without text labels, which many users cannot interpret.
Error messages that blame the user ('Wrong input!') instead of explaining the fix.
No confirmation for actions that cost money or delete data.
Forgetting what happens when the network fails halfway through a task.

blocks.text: Heuristic reviews have limits. You already know how your design is meant to work, so you will miss problems that confuse a first-time user. You may also judge something as a problem that real users handle easily. That is why the next step in this module is testing with real people. Use the review to clean up the obvious issues first, so your test participants spend their time revealing the problems you could not see.

blocks.title: Keep the list handy
blocks.text: Print or save the 10 heuristics on your phone. Use them as a checklist every time you finish a set of wireframes.

takeaways: Nielsen's 10 heuristics are a quick checklist for finding usability problems
Record screen, problem, heuristic broken, fix and severity for each issue
Severity 4 and 3 problems are fixed first
Heuristic reviews complement, but never replace, testing with real users

activity.title: Review your prototype
steps: Open your clickable prototype from Module 2 and go through your main task twice.
List every problem you find with the screen, the heuristic broken and a suggested fix.
Rate each problem from 0 to 4.
Ask one other person to do the same review separately, then combine both lists.
Fix all severity 3 and 4 problems in Figma.
activity.evidence: Your heuristic review table (problem, heuristic, severity, fix) and before-and-after screenshots of at least one fixed screen.

lessons.title: Accessible, inclusive and ethical design
objectives: Explain the four WCAG principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust
Apply key accessibility checks: colour contrast, text size, labels, touch targets and alt text
Design for low literacy, multiple languages and low data
Recognise deceptive design patterns and handle user data responsibly

blocks.text: **Accessibility** means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use your product. This includes people who are blind or have low vision, are deaf or hard of hearing, have limited hand movement, or have cognitive or learning disabilities. It also helps everyone else: an older aunt with weaker eyesight, a mother holding a baby in one arm, someone in bright sunshine at a bus stop.

The international standard is the **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)**, published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). The current version is WCAG 2.2. Its success criteria have levels A, AA and AAA; most organisations aim for **level AA**. WCAG is organised under four principles, often remembered as **POUR**.

blocks.title: WCAG principles (POUR)
items: Perceivable: can sense it
Operable: can use controls
Understandable: clear and predictable
Robust: works with assistive tech
blocks.caption: Every accessibility check you do fits under one of these four principles.

blocks.text: Practical checks you can do today

head: Check
What to look for
WCAG basis
rows: Normal text at least 4.5:1 against its background; large text at least 3:1. Use a free contrast checker.
Errors shown with text or an icon, not only a red border
Meaningful images have alt text describing their purpose
Every form field has a visible label, not just placeholder text that disappears
Tappable targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough space around them

blocks.name: eyeglasses
blocks.caption: Strong contrast and readable text help users with weaker eyesight, and everyone in bright sunlight.

blocks.text: Designing for real Nigerian users

items: **Low literacy:** use short, common words, pair icons with text labels, and consider voice notes or audio help, which many people already use on WhatsApp.
**Languages:** if your users prefer Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo or Yoruba, test whether key labels should be translated. Never assume English alone is enough.
**Low data and older phones:** compress images, avoid auto-playing video, and make sure the core task works on a small, older Android screen.
**Shared phones:** some users share a phone with family. Do not show sensitive information on the lock screen, and make logging out easy.
**Screen readers:** blind users often use TalkBack on Android or VoiceOver on iPhone. Buttons need real names, so the reader says 'Pay now' instead of 'Button'.

blocks.text: Ethics: no deceptive design

**Deceptive patterns** (also called dark patterns, a term coined by designer Harry Brignull) are design tricks that push people into choices they did not intend. Examples include hidden costs that appear only at the last step, pre-ticked boxes that sign people up for things, 'confirmshaming' buttons such as 'No thanks, I don't want to save money', and making cancellation much harder than sign-up. They may raise short-term numbers but destroy trust, and some may break consumer or data protection rules.

blocks.title: Worked example: making a loan app screen honest and accessible
blocks.context: For example, Aisha is asked to review the sign-up screen of a small savings and loan app aimed at market traders.
steps: She finds light grey text on white. A contrast checker shows about 2.3:1, below the 4.5:1 minimum, so she darkens it.
Form fields use placeholder text only ('Enter phone') that vanishes when typing. She adds visible labels above each field.
A box saying 'Allow access to my contacts' is pre-ticked. She unticks it and adds a plain explanation of why the app asks and that saying no is fine.
Interest and fees appear only after the user accepts. She moves the total repayment amount onto the screen before acceptance.
The error for a wrong phone number is only a red outline. She adds the text 'Phone number should have 11 digits, for example 0803 123 4567'.
blocks.result: Five changes make the screen readable, clear and honest. Users can make an informed choice, which also protects the business's reputation.

blocks.text: Inclusive design is also about who you include in research. If every participant is a young, confident smartphone user in Lagos, your design may fail an older trader in Kano or a first-time smartphone owner in a rural area. Plan your participants so that the people most likely to struggle are part of every round of testing. Their feedback usually improves the product for everyone.

blocks.title: Ask only for data you need
blocks.text: Under Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, personal data should be collected for a clear purpose and kept secure. In design terms: ask for the minimum, explain why you ask, make permissions optional where possible, and never hide consent inside long terms.

takeaways: WCAG 2.2 level AA is the common target; its principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, robust
Check contrast (4.5:1 for normal text), labels, alt text, target size and not relying on colour alone
Design for low literacy, local languages, low data and shared phones
Avoid deceptive patterns; collect only the data you need and explain why

activity.title: Accessibility and ethics audit
steps: Run your prototype through the six checks in the table above.
Use a free online contrast checker on your main text and button colours.
Read every label and error message aloud; rewrite any that use jargon.
Look for any deceptive pattern, pre-ticked box or hidden cost and remove it.
Ask one person who is older or has weaker eyesight to try one task and note what they say.
activity.evidence: A completed six-point accessibility checklist, contrast checker results, and before-and-after screenshots of at least two fixes.

lessons.title: Usability testing with 5 users and measuring results
objectives: Plan a usability test with realistic task scenarios
Moderate a think-aloud session without leading the participant
Measure task success, time on task, errors and System Usability Scale (SUS) scores
Write a short findings report that others can act on

blocks.text: A **usability test** means watching real users try to complete real tasks with your design. You do not ask them what they think of it; you observe what they do. It is the single most valuable UX method, because it shows where the design fails in ways that neither you nor a heuristic review would predict.
Why five users?

In a well-known NN/g article, Jakob Nielsen showed that testing with about **5 users** reveals roughly 85 percent of the usability problems in a design, for qualitative testing. After that, each extra user mostly shows you problems you have already seen. His advice is to run several small rounds: test with 5, fix the problems, then test again with another 5. This finds more problems overall than one big test with 15 people.

blocks.title: Small rounds of testing
items: Test with 5 users
List and rate problems
Fix the worst ones
Test again
blocks.caption: Repeated small tests find more problems than one big test, because each round checks the fixes.

blocks.text: Planning the test

items: Write 3 to 5 **task scenarios** that match real goals. Give context without telling them which button to press: 'You want knotless braids this Saturday morning. Book a time.' Not: 'Tap Book, then tap Saturday.'
Recruit 5 participants who match your persona, using your consent script.
Prepare your prototype link and a note sheet with one column per task.
Decide what you will measure (see the table below).

blocks.text: During the session

Ask the participant to **think aloud**: say what they are looking at, thinking and trying to do. Your job is to watch and listen. If they ask 'What should I press?', reply 'What would you do if I were not here?' Do not explain the design or rescue them too quickly. Note where they hesitate, what they tap, what they say, and whether they succeed. If you can, ask a colleague to take notes while you guide.

head: Metric
How to measure
Example result
rows: Number who completed the task without help, divided by number who tried
Seconds from start to completion, for those who succeeded
Count of wrong taps, wrong paths or mistakes
10-question System Usability Scale questionnaire after the test, scored 0 to 100

blocks.text: The **System Usability Scale (SUS)**, created by John Brooke, is a standard 10-statement questionnaire answered on a 5-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. The answers convert to a score from 0 to 100. It is not a percentage. Research by Jeff Sauro suggests an average score is around 68, so scores above that are better than average. With only 5 users, treat SUS as a rough signal, not proof.

blocks.name: usability-testing
blocks.alt: A person testing an app while another person observes and takes notes
blocks.caption: In a usability test you watch what people do, not just what they say.

blocks.title: Worked example: before and after one round of fixes
blocks.context: For example, Blessing tests her salon booking prototype with 5 customers, fixes the worst problems, then tests a new version with 5 different customers.
steps: Round 1: 3 of 5 completed the booking without help (60%). Average time for those 3: 95 seconds. 11 errors in total.
Top problem: 4 of 5 did not notice the deposit amount until the payment screen. Severity 3.
She adds the deposit amount to the style selection screen and makes the 'Confirm' button larger and lower on the screen.
Round 2: 5 of 5 completed without help (100%). Average time: 48 seconds. 3 errors in total.
Average SUS rose from 58 in round 1 to 77 in round 2.
blocks.result: Success went from 60% to 100% and time roughly halved. These before-and-after numbers become strong evidence in her final report and portfolio.

blocks.text: Writing the findings report

Keep it short enough to read in five minutes: what you tested and with whom (codes, not names), the tasks, the key numbers, the top 3 to 5 problems with severity, a screenshot or quote for each, and your recommended fixes. Lead with the most serious problems. Include at least one thing that worked well, so the team knows what to keep.

Remote testing works well when meeting in person is hard. Share the prototype link on WhatsApp, start a video call, and ask the participant to share her screen if her phone allows it, or to describe aloud what she sees and taps. Expect some sessions to drop because of network problems, so book one extra participant per round. Always repeat your consent script at the start of a remote session.

blocks.title: Do not over-claim
blocks.text: Five users show you problems; they do not prove percentages for a whole population. Write '4 of 5 participants' rather than '80% of users', and avoid big claims from small samples.

takeaways: Test with about 5 users per round, fix, then test again
Give realistic scenarios, ask people to think aloud, and do not lead them
Measure success rate, time on task, errors and SUS
Report findings with counts, severity, evidence and clear recommendations

activity.title: Run your usability test
steps: Write 3 task scenarios for your prototype.
Test with 5 participants who match your persona, using think-aloud.
Record success, time, errors and a SUS score for each participant.
Fix the top problems in Figma, then test the new version with at least 3 more people.
Write a one-page findings report with before-and-after numbers.
activity.evidence: Your test note sheets, a results table for both rounds, and a one-page findings report with recommended fixes.

quiz.q: A wallet app shows the recipient's account name before you confirm a transfer. Which heuristic does this mainly support?
quiz.explain: Showing the name lets users catch a wrong account number before the money leaves, which prevents a serious error.

quiz.q: During a review, Tunde finds that a payment page shows a blank screen for 30 seconds after 'Pay', and people pay twice. What severity should he give it?
quiz.explain: It causes real financial loss and happens often, so it must be fixed before release.

quiz.q: A design uses grey text on a white background with a contrast ratio of 2.5:1 for normal body text. What does WCAG level AA require?
options: Any contrast is fine if the font is nice
quiz.explain: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 for large text) at level AA.

quiz.q: Which of these is a deceptive design pattern?
options: Showing the full price before checkout
A pre-ticked box that signs users up for paid extras
quiz.explain: Pre-ticked boxes push users into choices they did not actively make, which is a recognised deceptive pattern.

quiz.q: Kemi has budget to test with 15 people. Following Nielsen's advice, what is the better plan?
options: Test all 15 at once, then fix everything
Run three rounds of 5 users, fixing problems between rounds
Skip testing and do a heuristic review
quiz.explain: Small repeated rounds find more problems overall because each round checks whether the previous fixes worked.

quiz.q: During a test, the participant asks, 'Which button should I press?' What should the facilitator say?
options: 'Press the green one at the bottom.'
'What would you do if I were not here?'
quiz.explain: Guiding the participant hides the real problem. Turning the question back keeps the test honest.

quiz.q: In Round 1, 3 of 5 users booked successfully. In Round 2, after fixes, 5 of 5 did. How should this be reported?
options: 'Success improved from 3 of 5 to 5 of 5 participants.'
'The app now works for 100% of Nigerians.'
quiz.explain: Report small-sample results as counts of participants and avoid claims about whole populations.

modules.title: Portfolio, Value and Next Steps
modules.overview: Bring your work together into a research pack and polished prototype, present it as a case study for employers, clients or communities, and finish with a certification check and a realistic 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Assemble your UX research pack and final prototype
objectives: Organise all your project evidence into a clear UX research pack
Raise your tested wireframes to a clean, consistent visual prototype in Figma
Use Figma components and simple styles to keep screens consistent
Check the final prototype against a quality checklist before submission

blocks.text: You now have the pieces of a real UX project: a problem statement, interview notes, themes, a persona, a journey map, a user flow, wireframes, a heuristic review, an accessibility audit, and test results. This lesson brings them together into two things: a **UX research pack** that shows your thinking, and a **final prototype** that shows the improved design.

blocks.name: complete-design
blocks.alt: A person finishing a completed screen design
blocks.caption: Your final project joins research, design and test evidence into one finished piece.

blocks.text: What goes in the research pack

head: Section
Contents
Source lesson
rows: Problem statement and 'How might we' question
Interview guide, number of participants, themes with counts
Current-state journey map, card sort result, user flow
Tasks, results for each round, findings report

blocks.text: Write a short introduction at the top of the pack: one paragraph stating the problem, who you worked with, how many people you interviewed and tested with, and the main result. Many readers will only read that paragraph, so make it complete. Put it in one shared folder (for example Google Drive) or a single PDF. Use participant codes, not names, and remove anything that identifies people unless you have their written permission.
From wireframe to visual prototype

Only now, after the structure has been tested, should you add visual design. Keep it simple and consistent. You are not trying to win an art prize; you are making the tested design clear and pleasant.

items: **Choose a small colour palette:** one main colour for primary buttons, one accent, neutral greys for text and backgrounds, plus a red for errors and green for success. Check contrast for every text colour.
**Choose one font family** with two or three sizes: a heading size, a body size and a small size. Many designers use a free Google Font such as Inter or Roboto.
**Make components:** design a button once, select it and choose 'Create component' in Figma. Reuse instances everywhere. When you change the main component, every copy updates.
**Save styles:** save your colours and text sizes as styles or variables so you pick from a set list instead of guessing.
**Replace placeholders** with realistic content: real hairstyle names, real-looking prices marked as examples, and fake but realistic phone numbers.

blocks.title: Worked example: Blessing's final submission
blocks.context: For example, Blessing finishes her salon booking project after two rounds of testing.
steps: She builds a button component (main, secondary, disabled) and an input field component (empty, filled, error) in Figma.
She applies a palette of one deep purple for primary actions, grey text, white backgrounds, red for errors and green for success, checking that every text colour passes 4.5:1.
Her final prototype has 6 screens, including an error screen for 'slot just taken' and a payment failure screen.
She tests the visual version quickly with 3 customers to make sure the new colours did not hide anything. All 3 complete the booking.
Her research pack is a 14-page PDF with the seven sections, plus a link to the Figma prototype.
blocks.result: The pack shows not just a pretty screen but the evidence behind every decision, which is what clients and employers want to see.

blocks.title: Final prototype quality check
items: Main task works end to end
Error and empty states included
Contrast passes 4.5:1
Labels on every field
Consistent components used
blocks.caption: Do not submit until every item on this checklist is true.

blocks.title: Show the before and after
blocks.text: Keep screenshots of your first wireframes and the original product or process. Side-by-side comparisons, backed by your test numbers, are the most convincing part of any UX project.
Common last-minute problems

items: Broken prototype links: test the share link while logged out, or on someone else's phone.
New visual styling that lowers contrast or makes buttons look like plain text.
Inconsistent spacing or button styles that crept in while fixing problems.
Personal data of participants left in screenshots or notes.

blocks.text: Design for every state

Real apps have more than one version of each screen. For every important screen, check that you have designed the **empty state** (for example, no bookings yet), the **loading state** (what she sees while the network works), the **error state** (what went wrong and how to fix it) and the **success state** (clear confirmation with a reference). Reviewers often judge a designer's maturity by whether these states exist, because they are where real users most often get stuck.

Set aside at least one full session for this final assembly. Read through the pack as if you were a busy manager seeing it for the first time: is the problem clear on page one, and can she find the prototype link in seconds?

takeaways: A research pack shows the evidence behind every design decision
Add visual design only after the structure has been tested
Use Figma components and saved styles for consistency
Check links, contrast, error states and privacy before submitting

activity.title: Build your pack and final prototype
steps: Create a folder or PDF with the seven sections from the table.
Create button and input field components in Figma and apply them to all screens.
Apply a small colour palette and one font family, and check text contrast.
Do a quick final test with 3 people to confirm the visual version still works.
Run the five-point quality checklist and fix anything that fails.
activity.evidence: Your research pack (folder link or PDF), the final prototype link, and the completed quality checklist.

lessons.title: Present your UX work as a case study
objectives: Structure a UX case study: problem, process, solution, results, reflection
Tailor the story for an employer, a small business client, or a community or donor audience
Present results honestly using your test numbers
Prepare a 2-minute spoken summary of your project

blocks.text: Good UX work only creates value when others understand it. Employers hiring designers look for evidence of how you think, not just finished screens. Small business owners want to know whether your work will bring more customers or fewer complaints. Community leaders and donors want to see who benefits. A **case study** tells the story of your project in a way each audience can follow.

blocks.name: presenting
blocks.alt: A person presenting charts and screens to an audience
blocks.caption: A clear case study turns your research and test results into a story others can act on.

blocks.text: The case study structure

blocks.title: Case study story
items: The problem and users
Your role and constraints
Research and insights
Design and iterations
Results and reflection
blocks.caption: Follow this order so the reader understands why each design decision was made.

items: **The problem and users:** one or two sentences on who struggled with what. Include your persona summary.
**Your role and constraints:** what you did yourself, how long it took, and limits such as budget, devices or data.
**Research and insights:** how many people you interviewed and the top 2 or 3 themes, with a short quote.
**Design and iterations:** sketches, wireframes and what changed after testing. Show one before-and-after.
**Results and reflection:** your test numbers and what you would do next or differently.

blocks.text: Tailor it to the audience

head: Audience
What they care about
What to lead with
rows: Research methods, iterations, what you learned
Customers, sales, time saved, fewer complaints
Before-and-after numbers and the business problem fixed
Who is helped and how fairly
Inclusion, accessibility, real user stories (with consent)

blocks.title: Worked example: one project, three openings
blocks.context: For example, Blessing prepares three versions of the first paragraph of her salon booking case study.
steps: For a design agency job: 'I led research and design for a salon booking flow. Six interviews revealed that unclear prices and slow WhatsApp replies were the main pain points. After two rounds of testing, task success rose from 3 of 5 to 5 of 5 participants.'

For the salon owner: 'Customers told us they wait hours for replies and are surprised by prices. In testing, the new booking page cut booking time from about 95 seconds to about 48 seconds, and every tester booked without help.'
For a women's business network: 'This simple booking page helps small salon owners take bookings while they work, and was tested with older customers and first-time smartphone users.'
Each version uses the same evidence but leads with what that reader values.
blocks.result: The facts never change; only the order and emphasis change. This keeps her honest while making the work relevant to each audience.

blocks.text: Be honest about results

Use the exact numbers from your tests and say how many participants were involved. Say what you did not test. If your project was a practice project and not launched, say so clearly: 'concept project, tested with 8 participants'. Employers respect honesty and will ask about it in interviews. Never present someone else's design as your own, and if your work was for a client, ask before showing it publicly.

blocks.title: Protect confidential work
blocks.text: If a client or employer asked you to keep their work private, do not post it. You can describe your process in general terms or recreate a similar example with changed details.
Presenting live

Sometimes you will present in person or on a video call. Keep slides few and visual: one slide for the problem, one for what you learned from users, two or three for the design and its changes, one for results and one for next steps. Show the prototype live if the connection is reliable, but keep screenshots ready in case the network fails. End by asking a clear question, such as 'Which of these fixes should we build first?', so the meeting leads to a decision.

Expect questions such as 'How did you choose participants?', 'What would you do with more time?' and 'What did you get wrong?'. Prepare short, honest answers. Saying 'In round one, my price layout confused four of five people, so I changed it' shows strength, not weakness.
Where to publish

You can share a case study as a PDF, on a free portfolio site such as Behance, on a simple personal website, or as a LinkedIn post with images. Keep images light so the page loads on mobile data. Put your best one or two projects first; two strong case studies are better than six weak ones. Add a short line about yourself and how to contact you at the end of each case study.

blocks.title: Practise a 2-minute summary
blocks.text: Prepare to explain your project out loud in about two minutes: the problem, what you learned from users, the key change you made, and the result. Record yourself on your phone and listen back.

takeaways: Case studies follow problem, role, research, design, results and reflection
Lead with what each audience values, but keep the facts the same
Report real numbers with participant counts and state what was not tested
Respect confidentiality and keep portfolio pages light for mobile data

activity.title: Write your case study
steps: Write your case study using the five-part structure, in 600 to 1,000 words with images.
Write two different opening paragraphs for two different audiences.
Include one before-and-after image and your test results table.
Record a 2-minute spoken summary on your phone.
Ask one person to read the case study and tell you, in one sentence, what problem you solved.
activity.evidence: Your case study (PDF or link), two opening paragraphs, the 2-minute recording, and the reader's one-sentence summary.

lessons.title: Certification checklist and your 90-day UX plan
objectives: Check your capstone evidence against the certification requirements
Compare common UX career paths and choose a direction
Write a realistic 90-day plan with weekly actions and measurable targets
Identify trustworthy free resources for continued learning

blocks.text: To earn your certificate you must complete the practical capstone and score at least 70 percent in the final quiz. Before you start the quiz, check your evidence honestly. A certificate is most useful when it is backed by work you can show and explain.

blocks.title: Certification evidence
items: Research pack complete
Prototype link works
Test results both rounds
Case study written
90-day plan done
blocks.caption: Each item must exist and be your own work before you attempt the final quiz.

blocks.text: UX career paths

head: Role
Focus
Good fit if you enjoy
rows: Flows, wireframes, prototypes, visual design, working with developers
Solving problems visually and seeing products ship
Interviews, usability testing, surveys, analysing findings
Listening to people and finding patterns
Labels, error messages, onboarding text, help content
Choosing clear words that guide people
Booking pages, online stores, forms, WhatsApp flows

blocks.name: certification
blocks.caption: Your certificate matters most when it sits beside real evidence of your work.

blocks.text: Building your 90-day plan

Whichever path you choose, the core skills are the same ones you practised in this course: understanding users, structuring content, prototyping and testing. In job adverts you will often see 'product designer' used for roles that combine UX and visual design. Read several adverts for the role you want and list the skills that appear most often; compare that list with your case studies to see your gaps.

Ninety days is long enough to grow a lot and short enough to stay focused. Split it into three 30-day blocks, each with one main goal, weekly actions and a number you can check. Be realistic about your time: if you have 5 hours a week, plan for 5 hours, not 20.

blocks.title: Worked example: Halima's 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Halima is a mother of two in Abuja with about 6 hours a week for UX practice. She wants to do paid freelance UX work for small businesses.
steps: Days 1 to 30, goal: a second case study. Weekly actions: 2 hours of research, 3 hours of design, 1 hour of reading NN/g articles. Target: second project tested with 5 users.

Days 31 to 60, goal: a real client. Weekly actions: offer a free or low-cost heuristic review to 2 local businesses per week through her network. Target: 1 business agrees and gives a written testimonial.

Days 61 to 90, goal: first paid project. Weekly actions: publish her two case studies, share one LinkedIn post each week about a UX lesson, and write a simple one-page service offer. Target: 1 paid project agreed with a written scope and deposit.
Every Friday she spends 15 minutes ticking off actions and noting what to change next week.
blocks.result: Each 30-day block has one goal and a clear number, so Halima can see progress and adjust instead of feeling lost.

blocks.text: Trustworthy places to keep learning

items: **Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com):** free articles and short videos on almost every UX topic, including the heuristics and testing methods in this course.
**W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (w3.org/WAI):** free, authoritative guidance on WCAG and accessible design.
**Figma Help Center and Figma's own learning resources:** official tutorials for every feature you will use.
**Google UX Design Professional Certificate on Coursera:** a longer structured programme if you want a deeper, portfolio-based course; check current pricing and financial aid options on Coursera.

blocks.title: Watch out for job and training scams
blocks.text: Be careful with offers that ask you to pay for a 'guaranteed job' or to pay before receiving work. Real clients agree a written scope first. When you freelance, take a deposit through a traceable channel such as a bank transfer or a Paystack payment link, and keep written records of what was agreed.
Keep your skills growing

UX skills grow through repetition. Each new project should stretch one skill: interview more varied users, try a card sort online, test with someone who uses a screen reader, or practise writing clearer error messages. Join a design community where people give honest feedback, and give feedback to others too, because reviewing other people's work trains your eye. Keep a simple learning log of what you tried each week and what you learned from it.
When you freelance

Write a short scope for every job: the problem, what you will deliver (for example a heuristic review report and 5 redesigned screens), the timeline, number of revision rounds, the price, and the payment schedule. Price by project rather than by the hour while you are new, and raise your prices as your case studies grow. Ask every happy client for a short testimonial you may quote, and keep copies of all agreements and receipts in one folder.

takeaways: Check all capstone evidence before attempting the final quiz (70% to pass)
Common paths: UX or product designer, UX researcher, UX writer, freelance UX
Plan in three 30-day blocks, each with one goal, weekly actions and a target number
Use trustworthy free sources and protect yourself with written scopes and deposits

activity.title: Finish and plan ahead
steps: Go through the certification checklist and fix anything missing.
Choose one career direction from the table and write two sentences on why.
Write your 90-day plan in three 30-day blocks with weekly actions and one target each.
Put a 15-minute weekly review in your phone calendar.
Take the final quiz.
